newsitem.title: USA: Bone marrow transplants lead to risk of new tumors.
newsitem.headline: Bone marrow transplants lead to risk of new tumors.

text.p: The cancer rate among people who survive a bone marrow transplant is eight times higher than it is for the general population and the risk is much greater for those who got their transplant as a child, a study concludes.

Such transplants, in which drugs or radiation are used to wipe out the bone's blood-producing marrow cells, which are then replaced by donated marrow, are usually attempted only when patients are likely to die without them.
The findings, reported in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, do not argue against performing the transplants. But the new research tells doctors more of the risks involved.

A team led by Rochelle Curtis of the National Cancer Institute analyzed nearly 20,000 transplant cases and found those who survived for at least 10 years faced a cancer risk that was 8.3 times higher than in the general population.
When the transplant was done before age 10 the cancer risk was significantly higher: nearly 27 times the rate in the general population.

Some types of tumors, known as solid tumors because they appear in a solid mass of errant cells at a specific spot in the body, were more common than others in survivors of bone marrow transplants. They included cancers of the brain, thyroid, bone, liver, skin, and parts of the mouth.
The study found no link between the transplant cases and cancers of the colon, rectum, breast, cervix, uterus or testes.

The more radiation the patient received during the treatment, the greater the cancer risk, the team concluded. The higher rates of cancers in thyroid, bone, brain, connective tissue and salivary gland seemed consistent with the effects of radiation.

But other factors such as changes in the immune system caused by the treatments used to prepare the body for the transplant, plus treatments initially given to a patient in hopes of killing the cancer before a transplant is attempted, probably contributed to the higher cancer rate as well, they said.
Curtis and her colleagues said the benefits of bone marrow transplants far outweigh the risks but they recommended that recipients be checked regularly for early signs of cancer.
"Bone marrow transplantation prolongs survival or is curative in many patients with cancer or other life-threatening diseases. These benefits clearly outweigh the risk," they said.

"However, our results should alert physicians that recipients of bone marrow transplants, particularly those receiving transplants at a young age, have an increased incidence of new solid cancers and that the excess risk of cancer rises sharply with time."

In an editorial in the Journal, Drs. David Schenkein of the New England Medical Center and Robert Schwartz, a deputy editor, said the findings "parallel the experience at Hiroshima and Nagasaki," where investigators discovered atomic bomb survivors from those cities were most likely to get cancer if they were younger than 10 years old at the time of the nuclear explosion.
In those cases, exposure to the radiation from the bomb blast was most likely to produce leukemia during the first five to seven years after the explosion.
